items.stem: Define the term 'mainframe computer'.
items.answer: A large, powerful computer used by organisations to process very large volumes of transactions and data reliably for many users at the same time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A large, powerful computer used by organisations to process very large volumes of transactions and data reliably for many users at the same time. [2]

items.stem: State what is meant by 'supercomputer'.
items.answer: A computer with very high processing speed, built from many processors working in parallel, used for complex calculations such as weather forecasting.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A computer with very high processing speed, built from many processors working in parallel, used for complex calculations such as weather forecasting. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a bank uses a mainframe computer to process transactions.
items.answer: A mainframe can process very large volumes of transactions for thousands of users at the same time, very reliably and securely, with almost no downtime.
items.markingKey: 1 mark large volume/many users; 1 mark reliability/availability/security. [2]

items.stem: Lotus Fashion, a clothing retailer with branches across the country, processes millions of customer transactions every day on a mainframe in Mexico City. Describe two characteristics of a mainframe computer.
items.answer: Reliability (rarely fails); availability (runs continuously); serviceability (repaired while running); very high input/output volumes; strong security; longevity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Kestrel Architects, an architecture practice in Bangkok, runs a mainframe for its customer transactions and has been asked to advise a national weather service on a new supercomputer. (a) Explain why the organisation needs high availability. (b) Describe one use of a supercomputer and explain why a supercomputer is needed for it.
items.answer: (a) Customers and staff need the service at all times; downtime would mean lost transactions, lost income and damaged reputation. (b) e.g. weather forecasting: complex models with billions of calculations must be completed before the forecast is out of date.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark continuous service; 1 mark consequence of downtime. [2] (b) 1 mark use; 1 mark reason (speed/complexity). [2]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the term 'RAS (reliability, availability, serviceability)'.
items.answer: Characteristics of a mainframe: it rarely fails, is almost always available, and can be repaired or upgraded while still running.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Characteristics of a mainframe: it rarely fails, is almost always available, and can be repaired or upgraded while still running. [2]

items.stem: Ines is writing a report for Nova Telecom in Madrid comparing mainframes and supercomputers. Describe two characteristics of a mainframe computer.
items.answer: Reliability (rarely fails); availability (runs continuously); serviceability (repaired while running); very high input/output volumes; strong security; longevity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Ines is writing a report for Kestrel Architects in Lagos comparing mainframes and supercomputers. (a) Explain why the organisation needs high availability. (b) Describe one use of a supercomputer and explain why a supercomputer is needed for it.

items.stem: Lina is writing a report for Sunrise Bakery in Auckland comparing mainframes and supercomputers. Discuss whether Sunrise Bakery should move its transaction processing from a mainframe to cloud servers.
items.answer: Points for: cloud is scalable, pay-as-you-go, no need to maintain hardware or specialist staff. Points against / limitations: mainframes offer proven reliability and security; data protection concerns over cloud; migration risks and costs; reliance on internet connection. Conclusion: for critical high-volume transaction processing, many organisations keep mainframes, possibly in a hybrid arrangement.

items.stem: Define the term 'compiler'.
items.answer: A translator that converts the whole of a high-level language program into machine code in one go, producing an executable file.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A translator that converts the whole of a high-level language program into machine code in one go, producing an executable file. [2]

items.stem: Explain two advantages of compiling a program before distributing it to customers.
items.answer: The executable runs faster because translation is done once; customers do not need the translator; the source code is not distributed so it cannot easily be copied or changed.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark point, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Explain why a programmer might use an interpreter during development.
items.answer: Errors are reported as soon as the line is reached, so they can be found and corrected easily; the program can be tested in parts without compiling the whole program.
items.markingKey: 1 mark errors located line by line; 1 mark quick testing/debugging. [2]

items.stem: Amara is a programmer at Silverline Couriers in Jakarta, writing a large application that will be sold to customers; Amara also looks after the office computers. Describe the purpose of a device driver for the new devices.
items.answer: Allows the operating system to communicate with the device by translating general commands into device-specific instructions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark OS–device communication; 1 mark device-specific. [2]

items.stem: Meridian Hospital in Dhaka has a small IT team that writes the organisation's own software and maintains its 150 office computers, scanners and printers. (a) Explain why a compiler would be used to produce the final version of the program. (b) Describe the role of a linker.
items.answer: (a) Produces an executable that runs quickly without the translator, and the source code is not given to customers. (b) Combines separately compiled modules and library routines into one executable program.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark executable/faster; 1 mark source code protected/no translator needed. [2] (b) 1 mark modules/libraries; 1 mark single executable. [2]

items.stem: The IT department of Starlight Cinemas in Lima is developing a new booking program and, at the same time, updating the software on all staff computers. Evaluate whether Starlight Cinemas should distribute its software as compiled executables or as source code run with an interpreter.
items.answer: Points for: compiled code runs faster and protects intellectual property; users need no translator. Points against / limitations: interpreted source runs on any platform with an interpreter and is easier to modify; compiled code must be recompiled for each platform. Conclusion: for commercial software sold to customers, compilation is usually preferred.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: compiled code runs faster and protects intellectual property; users need no translator. Against: interpreted source runs on any platform with an interpreter and is easier to modify; compiled code must be recompiled for each platform. Conclusion may argue: for commercial software sold to customers, compilation is usually preferred. [4]

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'linker' and 'compiler'.
items.answer: linker: System software that combines separately compiled modules (object code) and library routines into a single executable program. compiler: A translator that converts the whole of a high-level language program into machine code in one go, producing an executable file.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: linker correctly described; 1 mark: compiler correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain why a linker is needed.
items.answer: Large programs are written and compiled as separate modules and use library routines; the linker joins them into one executable, resolving references between them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark separate modules/libraries; 1 mark combined into single executable. [2]

items.stem: Explain why defragmenting a solid-state drive is not recommended.
items.answer: Access time on an SSD does not depend on where data is stored, so there is no speed benefit; unnecessary writes reduce the lifespan of the flash memory.
items.markingKey: 1 mark no speed gain (no moving parts); 1 mark extra writes reduce lifespan. [2]

items.stem: Which type of system software is used to scan files to detect and quarantine viruses?
items.answer: Anti-virus utility
items.markingKey: Anti-virus utility.

Name the type of system software needed for each task.

items.answer: 1 backup utility; 2 compiler; 3 disk formatter

items.stem: Define the term 'custom-written software'.
items.answer: Software written specially to meet the exact requirements of one client or organisation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Software written specially to meet the exact requirements of one client or organisation. [2]

items.stem: Explain two disadvantages of custom-written software.
items.answer: It is expensive because the whole development cost is paid by one client; it takes a long time to develop and test before it can be used; there may be bugs because it has few users.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark point, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Explain why off-the-shelf software is usually cheaper than custom-written software.
items.answer: The development cost is shared between thousands of customers, so each pays only a small part.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cost shared; 1 mark many users. [2]

items.stem: TransGlobal Logistics, a logistics company in Madrid, needs new software to manage its customer bookings and payments. Explain one risk of using proprietary software from a single supplier.
items.answer: Vendor lock-in: the organisation depends on the supplier for updates and prices; if the supplier stops supporting it, the organisation must change systems.
items.markingKey: 1 mark dependency; 1 mark consequence. [2]

items.stem: The directors of Atlas Museum in Auckland are deciding whether to buy an off-the-shelf package or pay FreshFarm Foods to write custom software. (a) Describe what is meant by open-source software. (b) Explain one risk of using proprietary software from a single supplier.
items.answer: (a) Software whose source code is available to view, modify and redistribute, usually free. (b) Vendor lock-in: the organisation depends on the supplier for updates and prices; if the supplier stops supporting it, the organisation must change systems.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark source available; 1 mark modify/share. [2] (b) 1 mark dependency; 1 mark consequence. [2]

items.stem: The directors of SwiftCar Rentals in Dhaka are deciding whether to buy an off-the-shelf package or pay Atlas Museum to write custom software. Assess the use of open-source software by SwiftCar Rentals.
items.answer: Points for: no licence cost; adaptable; large communities; not tied to one supplier. Points against / limitations: support can be limited; training costs; compatibility issues; may need in-house expertise. Conclusion: suitable if the organisation has technical staff or a support contract.

items.stem: State what is meant by 'off-the-shelf software'.
items.answer: Ready-made software that is available to buy or download and is designed for a general market of many users.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Ready-made software that is available to buy or download and is designed for a general market of many users. [2]

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'open-source software' and 'proprietary software'.
items.answer: open-source software: Software whose source code is made available so that users can study, modify and redistribute it, usually free of charge. proprietary software: Software owned by a company or individual; users buy a licence to use it but cannot see or change the source code.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: open-source software correctly described; 1 mark: proprietary software correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of open-source software for a business.
items.answer: Advantage: usually free and can be modified to fit needs. Disadvantage: support may be limited to online communities, and staff may need specialist skills to modify it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage + explanation; 1 mark disadvantage + explanation. [4]

items.stem: Explain why off-the-shelf software may contain features an organisation does not need.
items.answer: It is designed for a wide market, so it includes features for many different users, which makes it larger and possibly harder to learn.
items.markingKey: 1 mark general market; 1 mark consequence. [2]

items.stem: Atlas Museum in Jakarta needs software for 100 staff. Option A: custom-written software taking 1500 hours at $80 per hour, plus $3,000 per year maintenance. Option B: an off-the-shelf package at $300 per user licence, plus $150 per user per year for support. Calculate the total cost of each option over 3 years and state which is cheaper.
items.answer: A $129,000; B $75,000; B (off-the-shelf) is cheaper

items.stem: Northfield Academy in Doha needs software for 80 staff. Option A: custom-written software taking 1000 hours at $75 per hour, plus $4,000 per year maintenance. items.answer: A $87,000; B $40,800; B (off-the-shelf) is cheaper

items.stem: The directors of GreenLeaf Pharmacy in Mumbai are deciding whether to buy an off-the-shelf package or pay Harbour Bank to write custom software. (a) Explain two advantages of off-the-shelf software for this organisation. (b) Describe what is meant by open-source software.
items.answer: (a) Cheaper; available immediately; well tested with fewer bugs; lots of support, training and user forums. (b) Software whose source code is available to view, modify and redistribute, usually free.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each point, 1 mark each explanation, max 2 points. [4] (b) 1 mark source available; 1 mark modify/share. [2]

items.stem: Define the term 'command line interface (CLI)'.
items.answer: An interface in which the user types commands at a prompt, using exact syntax, to instruct the computer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: An interface in which the user types commands at a prompt, using exact syntax, to instruct the computer. [2]

items.stem: Explain two advantages of a GUI for a beginner.
items.answer: It is intuitive: users click icons and menus rather than remember commands; options are visible so less training is needed; help and undo are easy to find.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark point, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Explain why a command line interface is still used by network administrators.
items.answer: Commands give direct, fast access to all system functions and can be scripted to repeat tasks on many machines; it uses few resources and works over remote text connections.
items.markingKey: 1 mark speed/direct control; 1 mark scripting/remote/low resources. [2]

items.stem: Sunrise Bakery, a bakery in Santiago, is choosing the interface for a new information system used by staff and the public. Describe two features of a graphical user interface.
items.answer: Windows; icons; menus; pointer (WIMP); drag and drop; touch controls.

items.answer: (a) Windows; icons; menus; pointer (WIMP); drag and drop; touch controls. (b) Faster for experts; commands can be scripted and run on many computers; low resource use; access to all settings.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each, max 2. [2] (b) 1 mark point; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: Pioneer Insurance, an insurance company in Lagos, is choosing the interface for a new information system used by staff and the public. Discuss whether Pioneer Insurance should use a dialogue (voice) interface instead of a graphical user interface for its public information system.
items.answer: Points for: hands-free; accessible to people with visual impairment; natural for occasional users. Points against / limitations: background noise; accents and languages; privacy of spoken queries; a GUI shows options clearly. Conclusion: a combined interface (GUI with optional voice) is likely to suit most users.

items.stem: The directors of Starlight Cinemas in Manila are deciding whether to buy an off-the-shelf package or pay SkyLink Airways to write custom software. (a) Describe what is meant by open-source software. (b) Explain one risk of using proprietary software from a single supplier.
items.answer: (a) Software whose source code is available to view, modify and redistribute, usually free. (b) Vendor lock-in: the organisation depends on the supplier for updates and prices; if the supplier stops supporting it, the organisation must change systems.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark source available; 1 mark modify/share. [2] (b) 1 mark dependency; 1 mark consequence. [2]

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'dialogue interface' and 'graphical user interface (GUI)'.
items.answer: dialogue interface: An interface in which the user communicates with the computer using spoken (or typed natural-language) words and the computer replies. graphical user interface (GUI): An interface that uses windows, icons, menus and a pointer (WIMP) so the user can interact by pointing and clicking or touching.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: dialogue interface correctly described; 1 mark: graphical user interface (GUI) correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain why a dialogue interface is useful in a car.
items.answer: The driver can give commands by voice without taking hands off the wheel or eyes off the road, which is safer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark hands-free/eyes-free; 1 mark safety. [2]

items.stem: Which type of user interface is most suitable for a network technician who needs to configure many servers quickly using scripts?
items.answer: Command line interface
items.markingKey: Command line interface best suits this user.

items.stem: Recommend a suitable user interface for each user and justify your choices: (1) a network technician who needs to configure many servers quickly using scripts; (2) a person with limited hand movement controlling smart lights at home.
items.answer: (1) command line interface; (2) dialogue (voice) interface.
items.markingKey: (1) command line interface [1] with reason linked to the user [1]; (2) dialogue (voice) interface [1] with reason linked to the user [1]. [4]

items.stem: Samuel is designing interfaces for the staff, the public and the technicians of GreenLeaf Pharmacy in Karachi. Discuss whether GreenLeaf Pharmacy should use a dialogue (voice) interface instead of a graphical user interface for its public information system.
items.answer: Points for: hands-free; accessible to people with visual impairment; natural for occasional users. Points against / limitations: background noise; accents and languages; privacy of spoken queries; a GUI shows options clearly. Conclusion: a combined interface (GUI with optional voice) is likely to suit most users.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: hands-free; accessible to people with visual impairment; natural for occasional users. Against: background noise; accents and languages; privacy of spoken queries; a GUI shows options clearly. Conclusion may argue: a combined interface (GUI with optional voice) is likely to suit most users. [4]

items.stem: State what is meant by 'MIPS'.
items.answer: Millions of instructions per second: a measure of processing speed often quoted for mainframe computers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Millions of instructions per second: a measure of processing speed often quoted for mainframe computers. [2]

items.stem: Describe two uses of supercomputers.
items.answer: Weather forecasting and climate research (solving complex models of the atmosphere); quantum mechanics / molecular modelling for drug research; simulating nuclear reactions; genetic analysis.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per use with brief description, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Lakeside College, a college with branches across the country, processes millions of customer transactions every day on a mainframe in Toronto. Describe one use of a supercomputer and explain why a supercomputer is needed for it.
items.answer: e.g. weather forecasting: complex models with billions of calculations must be completed before the forecast is out of date.
items.markingKey: 1 mark use; 1 mark reason (speed/complexity). [2]

items.stem: Kwame is writing a report for Silverline Couriers in Lisbon comparing mainframes and supercomputers. Discuss whether Silverline Couriers should move its transaction processing from a mainframe to cloud servers.
items.answer: Points for: cloud is scalable, pay-as-you-go, no need to maintain hardware or specialist staff. Points against / limitations: mainframes offer proven reliability and security; data protection concerns over cloud; migration risks and costs; reliance on internet connection. Conclusion: for critical high-volume transaction processing, many organisations keep mainframes, possibly in a hybrid arrangement.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: cloud is scalable, pay-as-you-go, no need to maintain hardware or specialist staff. Against: mainframes offer proven reliability and security; data protection concerns over cloud; migration risks and costs; reliance on internet connection. Conclusion may argue: for critical high-volume transaction processing, many organisations keep mainframes, possibly in a hybrid arrangement. [4]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the term 'linker'.
items.answer: System software that combines separately compiled modules (object code) and library routines into a single executable program.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: System software that combines separately compiled modules (object code) and library routines into a single executable program. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'device driver' and 'operating system'.
items.answer: device driver: Software that allows the operating system to communicate with and control a particular hardware device. operating system: System software that manages the computer's hardware and software resources and provides an interface for the user.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: device driver correctly described; 1 mark: operating system correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a linker is needed. (b) Explain why a programmer might use an interpreter during development.
items.answer: (a) Large programs are written and compiled as separate modules and use library routines; the linker joins them into one executable, resolving references between them. (b) Errors are reported as soon as the line is reached, so they can be found and corrected easily; the program can be tested in parts without compiling the whole program.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark separate modules/libraries; 1 mark combined into single executable. [2] (b) 1 mark errors located line by line; 1 mark quick testing/debugging. [2]

items.stem: The IT department of Lakeside College in Dhaka is developing a new booking program and, at the same time, updating the software on all staff computers. Explain why an interpreter might be used while the program is being written.
items.answer: Errors are found line by line so debugging is easier; code can be tested without compiling everything.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each. [2]

items.stem: The IT department of TransGlobal Logistics in Mexico City is developing a new booking program and, at the same time, updating the software on all staff computers. (a) Describe the purpose of a device driver for the new devices. (b) Describe two utilities that would help maintain the computers.
items.answer: (a) Allows the operating system to communicate with the device by translating general commands into device-specific instructions. (b) Anti-virus (detects/quarantines malware); backup (copies data for restoring); defragmenter (speeds HDD access); compression (saves space); disk cleanup.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark OS–device communication; 1 mark device-specific. [2] (b) 1 mark per utility with purpose, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Aisha is a programmer at BlueWave Supermarkets in Muscat, writing a large application that will be sold to customers; Aisha also looks after the office computers. Evaluate whether BlueWave Supermarkets should distribute its software as compiled executables or as source code run with an interpreter.
items.answer: Points for: compiled code runs faster and protects intellectual property; users need no translator. Points against / limitations: interpreted source runs on any platform with an interpreter and is easier to modify; compiled code must be recompiled for each platform. Conclusion: for commercial software sold to customers, compilation is usually preferred.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks developed points on one or both sides; 5-6 marks balanced, applied discussion with a justified conclusion. Indicative content — for: compiled code runs faster and protects intellectual property; users need no translator. Against: interpreted source runs on any platform with an interpreter and is easier to modify; compiled code must be recompiled for each platform. Conclusion may argue: for commercial software sold to customers, compilation is usually preferred. [6]

items.stem: Define the term 'open-source software'.
items.answer: Software whose source code is made available so that users can study, modify and redistribute it, usually free of charge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Software whose source code is made available so that users can study, modify and redistribute it, usually free of charge. [2]

items.stem: Hana works for Meridian Hospital, a hospital in Jakarta, which plans to start switching from proprietary office software to an open-source office suite. Explain one disadvantage to the organisation of this.
items.answer: Staff need retraining.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: disadvantage identified, e.g. staff need retraining; file compatibility problems with partners; support relies on communities or paid third parties. 1 mark: explained in context. [2]

items.stem: Summit Engineering, an engineering firm in Santiago, needs new software to manage its customer bookings and payments. Explain one risk of using proprietary software from a single supplier.
items.answer: Vendor lock-in: the organisation depends on the supplier for updates and prices; if the supplier stops supporting it, the organisation must change systems.
items.markingKey: 1 mark dependency; 1 mark consequence. [2]

items.stem: Kestrel Architects in Mumbai needs software for 40 staff. Option A: custom-written software taking 1500 hours at $40 per hour, plus $5,000 per year maintenance. Option B: an off-the-shelf package at $200 per user licence, plus $120 per user per year for support. Calculate the total cost of each option over 3 years and state which is cheaper.
items.answer: A $75,000; B $22,400; B (off-the-shelf) is cheaper

items.stem: Summit Engineering, an engineering firm in Cairo, needs new software to manage its customer bookings and payments. Discuss the use of open-source software by Summit Engineering.
items.answer: Points for: no licence cost; adaptable; large communities; not tied to one supplier. Points against / limitations: support can be limited; training costs; compatibility issues; may need in-house expertise. Conclusion: suitable if the organisation has technical staff or a support contract.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: no licence cost; adaptable; large communities; not tied to one supplier. Against: support can be limited; training costs; compatibility issues; may need in-house expertise. Conclusion may argue: suitable if the organisation has technical staff or a support contract. [4]

items.stem: Distinguish between 'graphical user interface (GUI)' and 'command line interface (CLI)'.
items.answer: graphical user interface (GUI): An interface that uses windows, icons, menus and a pointer (WIMP) so the user can interact by pointing and clicking or touching. command line interface (CLI): An interface in which the user types commands at a prompt, using exact syntax, to instruct the computer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: graphical user interface (GUI) correctly described; 1 mark: command line interface (CLI) correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'dialogue interface' and 'command line interface (CLI)'.
items.answer: dialogue interface: An interface in which the user communicates with the computer using spoken (or typed natural-language) words and the computer replies. command line interface (CLI): An interface in which the user types commands at a prompt, using exact syntax, to instruct the computer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: dialogue interface correctly described; 1 mark: command line interface (CLI) correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Which type of user interface is most suitable for a young child using an educational app on a tablet?
items.answer: Gesture-based interface
items.markingKey: Gesture-based interface best suits this user.

items.stem: Horizon Travel, a travel agency in Riyadh, is choosing the interface for a new information system used by staff and the public. (a) Explain one disadvantage of a gesture-based interface. (b) Explain why the technicians might prefer a command line interface.
items.answer: (a) Unintended gestures may trigger commands; tiring; needs a camera/sensors; limited number of gestures recognised. (b) Faster for experts; commands can be scripted and run on many computers; low resource use; access to all settings.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark point; 1 mark explanation. [2] (b) 1 mark point; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: City Central Library, a library in Lagos, is choosing the interface for a new information system used by staff and the public. (a) Describe two features of a graphical user interface. (b) Compare a GUI and a CLI in terms of ease of learning and use of resources.
items.answer: (a) Windows; icons; menus; pointer (WIMP); drag and drop; touch controls. (b) GUI is easier to learn as options are visible; CLI requires memorising commands; GUI uses more memory and processing power.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each, max 2. [2] (b) 1 mark ease of learning; 1 mark resources. [2]
